items.title: John Bunch interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: I showed them to, I think it was Jake Hanna or somebody, and he said, “My, those are wonderful cymbals,”

ctx.x: I’m just off on this sideline. John you were talking about some of the people that had great stories that we talked to. And you mentioned Milt Hinton and Doc Cheatham. I take it that you know some of those stories? Do you? Would you share any of them?

Well I can’t think of many stories in relation to those two. I’m not a very good, I don’t have a very good memory. As far as, I was just telling some people today you know I also worked with Gene Krupa quite a lot in the quartet. With Charlie Ventura. He was one of the great guys, one of the nicest guys, personally. The complete opposite from these three guys that I worked long periods of time on. And I should put in a word, speaking of nice guys that had fame and everything, Woody Herman was another one that I…

items.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: But it was the first and sometimes the only record date with that company. And Mike Moore, and John Bunch. So we just threw it together.

ctx.x: How does it change your playing to work without a bass player?

Well you adjust the playing. Sometimes I just leave the hi hat off. And you play off the snare and the bass drum stays very steady. You’ve got to re-tune it where it gets a nice tone. And it all depends on that piano player see? You’ve got to have a nice, loose left © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

hand. Can’t be pounding. Teddy can play you know. There’s only one Teddy Wilson. And that’s Johnny Varro. But Johnny is very good, absolutely. And Ralph Sutton. We have a good, easy time with Ralph and we have an easy time with John Bunch, and Dave McKenna, he’s born for that, Dave McKenna is the king of that stuff. In fact he doesn’t need us. So the hell with Dave.
